basic_identification.name: Canyon Media Art Conservation Center (CMACC)
basic_identification.originator: Part of the Canyon museum ecosystem. Established as the first US nonprofit conservation center dedicated to time-based media art. Connected to broader media art conservation networks. Specific founding leadership details require verification. [uncertain]
basic_identification.geography: United States. Specific location tied to Canyon museum. Serves a national gap in media art conservation infrastructure. [uncertain]

core_ideas.core_claim: CMACC addresses the critical infrastructure gap in conservation of time-based and digital media art in the United States. While European institutions (Tate, ZKM, LIMA, RED Conservation Center) have developed media art conservation capacity, the US has lacked a dedicated nonprofit center for this purpose. CMACC provides specialized conservation services for artworks that include video, software, digital files, performance-based elements, and other time-based components — works that traditional conservation practices are not equipped to handle. [uncertain]
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Entirely medium-specific. CMACC exists because digital and time-based media art has fundamentally different conservation requirements than traditional art. Software becomes obsolete, hardware degrades, file formats become unreadable, platforms disappear. The center addresses conservation challenges unique to digital media: emulation, migration, format conversion, software dependency management, hardware lifecycle planning, and documentation of interactive and performative elements.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Resistant to attention economy. Conservation operates on deep-historical timescales incompatible with engagement metrics. The work is slow, technical, highly specialized, and largely invisible. CMACC's existence counters the attention economy's normalization of impermanence — it asserts that born-digital cultural production deserves the same preservation commitment as traditional media. This is infrastructure that operates entirely outside attention-economy logic.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Strongly intention-native. Conservation addresses the most fundamental structural need of the field: ensuring that digital artworks survive beyond their immediate technological context. CMACC serves declared long-term needs (preservation, access, knowledge continuity) rather than capturing engagement. This is perhaps the purest example of intention-aligned infrastructure in the digital art field.

market_economics.revenue_model: Nonprofit. Likely funded through a combination of foundation grants, institutional partnerships, museum consortium fees, government arts funding (NEA, state arts councils), and individual donations. May offer fee-for-service conservation to museums and private collectors. Revenue model for media art conservation centers is structurally challenging: the work is expensive, specialized, and does not generate market returns. [uncertain]
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure — entirely upstream of markets. Conservation enables the long-term value of media art but generates no direct market revenue. CMACC serves museums, artist estates, galleries, and potentially private collectors who hold time-based media works.
market_economics.price_range: N/A for art sales. Conservation services are cost centers, not revenue generators. Individual conservation projects for time-based media art can cost thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on complexity, technology requirements, and scale.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing need, severely insufficient capacity. The volume of time-based and digital media art requiring conservation grows exponentially as more artists work with digital tools and more institutions acquire digital works. CMACC represents a small but significant addition to capacity. The gap between conservation need and conservation capacity continues to widen across the field. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: N/A directly. CMACC serves institutions (museums, archives, university collections) and potentially artist estates and private collectors who hold time-based media art. The primary 'clients' are institutions with fiduciary responsibility to preserve their collections.
market_economics.sustainability: Structurally challenging under current models. Media art conservation is a public goods problem: it benefits the entire field but has no market mechanism for funding. Nonprofit grant dependency creates project-to-project uncertainty. Long-term sustainability requires either endowed funding, institutional consortium models that distribute costs, or integration into standard museum practice. The fact that CMACC is the first of its kind in the US underscores how under-resourced this field is. [uncertain]

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Media art conservation tools: Archivematica (digital preservation), BitCurator (born-digital curation), emulation software (EaaS — Emulation-as-a-Service), Webrecorder/Conifer (web archiving), MediaInfo (technical metadata extraction), QCTools (quality control for video), PRONOM (file format registry), Variable Media Questionnaire (documentation methodology), disk imaging tools, video format migration tools, hardware testing and maintenance equipment. Likely also custom tools for specific conservation challenges. [uncertain]
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Emerging and cautious. AI could assist with automated format identification, degradation detection, metadata extraction, and documentation of large collections. However, the conservation field is cautious about AI: can an AI-migrated artwork preserve the artist's intent? AI-generated art creates new conservation challenges (preserving works dependent on specific model versions, API access, or cloud services). CMACC will likely need to develop conservation approaches for AI-based artworks while potentially using AI as a conservation tool. [uncertain]
practice_aesthetics.liveness: CMACC conserves liveness. The artworks in its care are often live, interactive, performative, or generative. The central challenge of media art conservation is preserving the experience of liveness — not just preserving files but preserving the interactive, temporal, and behavioral dimensions of time-based works. Emulation attempts to preserve liveness by recreating original execution environments.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Technical-conservation: emulation, migration, reinterpretation, documentation, variable media, time-based media, significant properties, behavioral preservation, bit-level preservation, format migration, software dependency, hardware obsolescence, artist interview, installation specification, authenticity, integrity, reversibility, minimal intervention. The vocabulary bridges art conservation tradition with digital technology terminology.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Strongly open (conservation knowledge is shared through professional networks, publications, conferences). Strongly commons (conservation is a public good). Strongly infrastructure (this is definitional infrastructure). Collective (conservation of individual artworks through collective institutional effort and shared knowledge).

infrastructure_governance.openness: Likely open in knowledge sharing (conservation standards, methodologies, case studies shared through professional networks like INCCA, AIC). Conservation methods and findings are typically published and shared. Tools used are primarily open-source. Specific CMACC policies on openness require verification. [uncertain]
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Nonprofit governance: board of directors, executive leadership, advisory committees potentially including artists, conservators, technologists, and museum professionals. Connected to Canyon museum's broader governance structure. May participate in professional networks (AIC Electronic Media Group, INCCA, EMBARK). [uncertain]
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Conservation records and documentation are held by CMACC and shared with the artwork owners (institutions, artists, estates). Artist interviews and documentation become part of the conservation record. Metadata and technical documentation are created and maintained by the center. Data portability is important: if an institution removes a work from CMACC's care, the conservation documentation should transfer with it. [uncertain]
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Should interoperate with museum collection management systems, digital preservation standards (OAIS reference model, PREMIS metadata), and professional conservation networks. Standardized documentation formats enable knowledge transfer between conservation professionals. Integration with international conservation databases and registries. [uncertain]
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: This IS preservation strategy. CMACC's entire mission is preservation of time-based media art. Approaches likely include: emulation (recreating original technical environments), migration (converting to current formats), documentation (recording all technical and conceptual aspects), reinterpretation (allowing adaptation while maintaining artistic intent), and preventive conservation (maintaining hardware, monitoring format obsolescence). The center provides the infrastructure for implementing these strategies at scale.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Artist consent is central to conservation ethics. Conservation decisions (emulation vs. migration vs. reinterpretation) require artist input when the artist is living. The Variable Media Questionnaire and artist interview methodologies are consent frameworks: they document the artist's preferences for how their work should be preserved and adapted. The consent model is opt-in and granular: artists specify what can and cannot be changed. [uncertain]

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Integration. CMACC extends traditional conservation principles to digital media — it is a natural evolution of art conservation practice, not a disruption of it. Connected to the museum ecosystem through Canyon. Bridges the digital art world and the traditional conservation profession. Addresses a need that traditional art institutions recognize but have been unable to fill internally.
field_position.what_it_enables: Dedicated conservation services for time-based media art in the US (previously only available through individual museum departments or European centers). Professional development and training for media art conservators. Centralized expertise that smaller institutions can access. Research and development of conservation methodologies for emerging media types. A US anchor institution for the global media art conservation network.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Scale — one center cannot address the conservation needs of the entire US media art field. Funding sustainability — nonprofit conservation is chronically underfunded. Coverage of blockchain/NFT art conservation (this is likely a gap even for CMACC). International coordination capacity. Sufficient trained conservators (the field has a workforce shortage). Engagement with non-institutional collections (independent artists, community archives). [uncertain]
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists and institutions outside CMACC's geographic reach or financial capacity to access services. Emerging digital art forms that are too new or too niche for conservation protocols to exist. Artists working with proprietary platforms or cloud-dependent tools where conservation is technically impossible without platform cooperation. Non-Western media art practices that may not align with Western conservation ethics. Independent and self-taught digital artists without institutional connections. [uncertain]
field_position.frontier_signal: Frontier for the US (first dedicated nonprofit center of its kind). Established conceptually (media art conservation as a discipline is 25+ years old). The frontier is in institutionalization: turning scattered expertise into sustainable infrastructure. This is infrastructure-building in a field that has long recognized the need but lacked the institutional capacity.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Professional conservation networks (AIC, INCCA, EMBARK), museum and institutional channels, arts press (specialized), conference presentations, academic publications. Not discovered through social media or general press. Discovery is institutional and professional, not public-facing.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Near zero. Conservation infrastructure does not depend on public attention or engagement metrics. Its value is measured in artworks preserved, not in likes or clicks. CMACC would survive if all social media platforms disappeared — its mission is timescale-independent of attention cycles.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Maximally intention-aligned. Addresses the most fundamental structural need (preservation) without any attention-capture mechanism. This is pure infrastructure that serves the field's declared long-term requirements. The only 'audience' is future generations who will inherit the preserved artworks.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Strong. Conservation knowledge is shared through professional networks, publications, and training. Conservation methodologies developed by CMACC will benefit the entire field. The preserved artworks remain accessible to the public through their owning institutions. This is a direct contribution to cultural commons.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Both. Conservation documentation records ownership provenance (who holds the work, exhibition history) and meaning provenance (artist intent, conservation decisions, contextual documentation, technical evolution). The Variable Media approach explicitly documents the conceptual and experiential dimensions alongside the material/technical.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Deep-historical. Conservation operates on the longest timescale in the art world — ensuring artworks survive for future generations. The temporal logic is archival (preserving the past) and anticipatory (preparing for future technological changes). Conservation planning requires predicting future obsolescence and building resilience against it.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: CMACC directly addresses a critical absence: the lack of US-based nonprofit media art conservation infrastructure. Its existence makes other absences visible: the shortage of trained conservators, the lack of conservation standards for blockchain/AI art, the funding gap for preservation work. Conservation inherently deals with absence — its mission is to prevent the loss (absence) of cultural artifacts.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence. Conservation practice acknowledges that there are multiple valid approaches to preserving a work (emulation, migration, reinterpretation) and that the best approach depends on the specific work, artist intent, and institutional context. There is no single 'correct' way to conserve media art — the field seeks coherence (internally consistent approaches that respect the work) rather than consensus (one method for all).
coherence.contestability: High. Conservation decisions are inherently contestable: is emulation more authentic than migration? Does reinterpretation preserve or alter the work? Artists, conservators, curators, and scholars may disagree. The Variable Media approach provides a framework for structured disagreement (documenting different perspectives on conservation). Decisions can be revisited as technology and understanding evolve.
coherence.forkability: Moderate. Conservation methodologies are shared and can be adopted independently by any institution. However, the specialized equipment, expertise, and institutional infrastructure are difficult to replicate. The knowledge is forkable; the institutional capacity is not easily forked.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The principle that born-digital cultural artifacts require active, ongoing preservation (they do not preserve themselves). The Variable Media approach of documenting multiple dimensions (technical, conceptual, experiential) as a model for A(DAI)'s own record-keeping. The artist consent methodology (interviews, questionnaires) as a model for contributor engagement. The acceptance of multiple valid preservation approaches (coherence over consensus). The long-term temporal perspective that conservation demands.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The institutional gatekeeping that makes conservation access dependent on museum connections and funding. The Western-centric conservation ethics that may not apply to all cultural contexts. The scarcity model (one center, limited capacity) — A(DAI) should design for distributed preservation rather than centralized conservation. The separation of 'conservation' from 'creation' — A(DAI) should build preservation into its creation infrastructure from the start, not as an afterthought.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: CMACC preserves individual artworks through institutional expertise; A(DAI) must preserve field-level knowledge through distributed infrastructure. CMACC operates on the deep-historical timescale; A(DAI) operates on multiple temporal scales simultaneously (real-time sensing, archival, anticipatory). CMACC conserves what already exists; A(DAI) must also detect and represent what is absent. The productive tension: A(DAI) can learn CMACC's preservation rigor while applying it to a broader, more distributed, and more dynamic knowledge infrastructure.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Subject to nonprofit regulations (IRS 501(c)(3) or equivalent). Museum accreditation standards (AAM). Professional conservation ethics (AIC Code of Ethics). Copyright considerations when creating conservation copies of artworks. Export/import regulations for physical media components. Potential implications of EU AI Act if conservation processes involve AI-based tools. [uncertain]
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Conservation creates new IP (documentation, conservation reports, methodology publications) that is typically shared openly through professional channels. The artworks themselves retain their original IP status. Conservation copies may be subject to copyright exceptions for preservation (Section 108 of US Copyright Act). Institutional policies govern access to conservation documentation.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in. Conservation services are provided at the request of the artwork owner (institution, artist, estate). Artist participation in documentation (interviews, questionnaires) is voluntary. All conservation decisions require consent from the artwork owner and ideally the artist. This is an actively consent-based practice.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Low platform dependency. Conservation tools are primarily open-source. The center does not depend on any commercial platform for its core mission. However, conserving artworks that depend on specific platforms (social media works, cloud-based art, platform-specific software) requires engagement with those platforms, which represents a dependency for specific conservation projects rather than for CMACC itself.
ecosystem.network_effects: Moderate network effects. CMACC's value increases as more institutions participate (shared knowledge, shared costs, larger corpus of conservation case studies). The center serves as a hub in a network of museums, artists, and conservators. The value of conservation standards increases with adoption. However, conservation is not a platform — network effects are professional rather than platform-economic.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Not directly affected by the NFT crash. However, the crash underscored the impermanence of digital platforms and the need for preservation infrastructure independent of market cycles. Some NFT art may come to CMACC for conservation as institutions that acquired during the boom face preservation challenges. CMACC's establishment in the post-crash period reflects growing institutional recognition that digital art preservation cannot be left to market forces. [uncertain]
